 Associated Physicians Group Shares Advice as Patients Navigate Medicare Open Enrollment
 Insurance roadblocks can stand between patients and care their doctors prescribe. Associated Physicians Group shares what patients should know as they consider Medicare plans during open enrollment.
Sydney Sinks, News Reporter
Nov 19, 2026 11:34 AM
Nov 19, 2026 11:44 AM
 Save
 Listen to the story 
Your device does not support the audio.
Associated Physicians Group's Christina Rogerson on Medicare plan choices and navigating insurance barriers
 ALTON/EDWARDSVILLE/O’FALLON/SWANSEA - Associated Physicians Group is urging patients to advocate for themselves as insurance companies prepare for the open enrollment period.
 Sign in to hide this notification.

 Christina Rogerson, chief operating officer with APG, provided a few tips as people enroll in Medicare plans and consider their insurance options. She noted that it can be difficult to navigate insurance plans, and some people feel disconnected from their physicians because of the insurance “middleman.” She encourages people to talk to their physicians and insurance companies to ensure they get the treatment they need.
 Article continues after sponsor message 
 “There are a lot more gatekeepers, and it’s one of the complaints that I hear from patients all the time,” Rogerson said. “Twenty years ago, when you went in to see the doctor, you felt like your healthcare was being managed with a relationship between you and the physician. Now, patients feel like their healthcare is being managed with a middleman. And so it really begins to break down that patient-physician relationship that most patients value more than anything.”
 As Medicare open enrollment starts, Rogerson pointed to “a lot of waste, fraud and abuse within the Medicare system” that can make it more difficult for patients to access the care they need. But she emphasized that most “well-meaning, qualified providers” aren’t the ones contributing to this. Instead, patients and providers are often facing the same challenges.
 Rogerson noted that a lot of patients and physicians encounter “administrative roadblocks” that prevent people from getting the care their doctors have prescribed. Insurance companies often require many other tests or procedures before they will approve an MRI, for example. 
 Article continues after sponsor message 
 “Even if you want the service and your physician thinks the service is necessary, the insurance company can throw up hoops that the physician must first get through, and also the patient, before they can get that diagnostic approved,” she said. “It does really create challenges for the patient.”
 But Rogerson explained that physicians like those at APG will work with patients to ensure they receive the care they need. She pointed out that patients can often pay out of pocket, and providers will talk through your options with you in the case that your insurance denies treatment.
 Additionally, she encourages anyone who is struggling with insurance challenges to call their insurance company directly. Rogerson believes patients should be and deserve to be involved in their own care. 
 “I also always encourage patients to get involved and advocate for themselves,” she said. “Though providers can frequently do appeals if a service is denied or not approved, I always encourage patients to call their insurance company as well. At the end of the day, you have a relationship with that insurance company, and they should be advocating on your behalf.”
 Article continues after sponsor message 
 Whatever your situation is, APG can help you navigate your healthcare and insurance questions. With offices in Alton, Edwardsville, O’Fallon and Swansea, their team is always available and eager to assist. Rogerson encourages you to call 888-363-8333 or visit the official Associated Physicians Group website for more information.
